stem: A 52-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to increasing dyspnea and chest tightness over the past 2 weeks.  She has a history of stage 4 chronic kidney disease due to chronic glomerulonephritis.  Temperature is 36.6 C (97.8 F), blood pressure is 106/82 mm Hg, and pulse is 98/min.  Systolic blood pressure decreases by 12 mm Hg during inspiration.  Physical examination shows distant heart sounds and clear lungs.  Echocardiography in this patient is most likely to reveal which of the following findings?​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌

explanation:
Cardiac tamponade

Etiology

  • Blood in pericardial space (eg, left ventricular rupture, cardiac surgery)
  • Pericardial effusion (eg, malignancy, infection, uremia)

Clinical signs

  • Beck triad: hypotension, JVD, ↓ heart sounds
  • Pulsus paradoxus: >10 mm Hg drop in SBP during inspiration

Diagnosis

  • ECG: low-voltage QRS complex, electrical alternans
  • Chest x-ray: enlarged cardiac silhouette,* clear lungs
  • Echocardiogram: right atrial & ventricular collapse, IVC plethora

*Subacute but not acute tamponade.

IVC = inferior vena cava; JVD = jugular venous distension; SBP = systolic blood pressure.

This patient with progressive dyspnea, distant heart sounds, and a decrease in systolic blood pressure >10 mm Hg during inspiration (ie, pulsus paradoxus) most likely has subacute cardiac tamponade.  Uremia in advanced renal failure can cause pericarditis with an associated pericardial effusion, which can progress to tamponade.  Tamponade classically presents with Beck's triad of hypotension, distant heart sounds, and jugular venous distension, although hypotension may be less prominent when fluid accumulates gradually.

Normally, systemic venous blood flows into the right atrium along a pressure gradient.  During inspiration, decreased intrathoracic pressure lowers right atrial pressure, drawing more blood toward the heart.  Together with increased abdominal pressure from the descending diaphragm, this reduces the pressure holding the inferior vena cava (IVC) open, causing normal inspiratory narrowing (conventionally measured by echocardiography just below the diaphragm).

In cardiac tamponade, elevated pericardial pressure restricts cardiac filling, particularly in the right-sided chambers, where pressures are relatively low.  Increased right atrial pressure is transmitted backward to the systemic veins, causing enlargement of the IVC with decreased inspiratory collapse.

Elevated pericardial pressure also limits the total volume available to the cardiac chambers.  During inspiration, increased venous return expands the right ventricle, shifting the interventricular septum leftward and reducing the space available for left ventricular filling.  The resulting reduction in stroke volume causes pulsus paradoxus.  As tamponade progresses, impaired ventricular filling reduces cardiac output and can cause obstructive shock.  The lungs typically remain clear because impaired right ventricular filling limits blood flow into the pulmonary circulation, reducing the tendency for pulmonary edema.

(Choices A, B, D, and E)  Segmental (eg, apical) hypokinesis suggests myocardial ischemia or infarction, and dilation of all 4 cardiac chambers can occur with dilated cardiomyopathy.  Severe tricuspid regurgitation can occur with carcinoid syndrome.  Systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve is characteristic of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and contributes to left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.  These conditions do not typically produce the combination of pulsus paradoxus and distant heart sounds.

Educational objective:Cardiac tamponade occurs when elevated pericardial pressure restricts cardiac filling.  Increased right atrial pressure causes enlargement and decreased inspiratory collapse of the inferior vena cava.  Exaggerated competition between the ventricles for limited space reduces left ventricular filling during inspiration, producing pulsus paradoxus (>10 mm Hg inspiratory decrease in systolic blood pressure).​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌
